background.definition: Viral myocarditis is inflammation of the heart muscle caused by viral infection, which leads to viral cardiomyopathy. The clinical spectrum of viral myocarditis varies from asymptomatic to sudden cardiac death, fulminant myocarditis, and chronic dilated cardiomyopathy. Fulminant myocarditis presents with abrupt onset of severe heart failure, cardiogenic shock, and life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias.

list.listitem: Viral cardiomyopathy accounts for up to 10% of newly diagnosed cardiomyopathy that is confirmed by endomyocardial biopsy.
Myocardial inflammation was found in 9% of postmortem examinations in an older study.
It accounts for about 20% for sudden death in adults younger than 40 years and young athletes.
Sudden infant death syndrome can be due to viral myocarditis.

More common: enteroviruses such as coxsackie B, adenovirus, human immunodeficiency virus, parvo virus B19, hepatitis C, HIV and human herpes virus 6. Early variants of SARS-CoV-2 were thought to cause myocarditis. Viruses from the Coronaviridae family, such as the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus (SARS-CoV) and SARS-CoV-2, have angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) tropism and can potentially mediate direct cardiac injury.

Rare: cytomegalovirus, dengue virus, echo virus, encephalomyocarditis, Epstein-Barr virus, hepatitis A virus, influenza A and B viruses, Junin virus, lymphocytic choriomeningitis, measles, mumps, polio, rabies, respiratory syncytial virus, rubella, rubeola, vaccinia, varicella-zoster, variola, and yellow fever virus.
Other infectious causes: bacterial, fungal, spirochetal, protozoal, and parasitic.
Immune mediated: post heart transplant recipients, connective tissue diseases, allergic myocarditis, and idiopathic giant cell myocarditis.
Toxic myocarditis due to drugs, cancer treatment, and heavy metals.
Other acquired causes are endocrinopathies, pregnancy, liver cirrhosis and tachyarrhythmias.
Patients with HIV infection are more prone to dilated cardiomyopathy from HIV and superinfections from other viruses.
Inherited etiologies of cardiomyopathy are often overlooked in this population. 5-15% of patients with acquired dilated cardiomyopathy harbour a likely pathogenic gene mutation.

Based on animal studies, viral myocarditis can be divided into 3 phases. Phase 1 is viremia, which lasts for approximately 4 days. During this phase, viruses are taken into cardiac myocytes by receptor-mediated endocytosis and are translated to viral protein. The virus replicates inside the cell and later released into interstitium where phagocytosed by macrophages.

Phase 2 is viral clearing, which lasts for 10 days. The second phase characterized by infiltration of inflammatory cells such as natural killer cells, cytotoxic T, and B lymphocytes and release of cytokines such as interferon, interleukins, and expression of neutralizing antibodies (auto immune).
Finally, phase 3 is absence of virus, which lasts up to 3 months. The third phase is characterized by tissue destruction, myocardial fibrosis, cardiac dilatation, and heart failure.
Preliminary studies show that a cardiac myocyte cytoprotective effect against enterovirus is mediated through Gap protein 130 signaling. Gp 130 signaling is a possible future therapeutic target.
The clinical spectrum of viral cardiomyopathy varies from asymptomatic to sudden cardiac death, fulminant heart failure, and chronic dilated cardiomyopathy. C
Patients can present with flu-like symptoms followed by chest pain, palpitations, syncopal episode, dyspnea on exertion, and pedal edema. C
If clinically suspected, order ECG, creatine kinase, troponin T and I, and echocardiography. C
Cardiac MRI with gadolinium enhancement is useful for diagnosis and my preclude the need for endomyocardial biopsy.
Endomyocardial biopsy fulfilling Dallas criteria for myocarditis is the gold standard for diagnosis but has low sensitivity and is only recommended to exclude other causes of cardiomyopathy. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Can be differentiated only with myocardial biopsy
Cardiac catheterization to demonstrate coronary artery disease

list.listitem: Many patients are asymptomatic. Patients can present with flu-like prodromal symptoms followed by chest pain, palpitations, syncopal episode, dyspnea on exertion, and pedal edema. Viral prodromal symptoms are highly variable, occurring in 10% to 80%.
Physical examination may reveal signs of congestive heart failure such as jugular venous distension, crackles on lung exam, S3 gallop and peripheral edema.

Patients with fulminant myocarditis present with viral prodromal symptoms followed by acute heart failure symptoms, namely shortness of breath, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and pedal edema.
Obtain a thorough family history to exclude familial cardiomyopathy. Viral prodromes are non-specific, and do not fully exclude an inherited basis for cardiomyopathy.

When viral cardiomyopathy is clinically suspected, order cardiac troponins, CK-MB, C-reactive protein, CBC with differential, CXR, ECG, and echocardiogram. Laboratory testing may show leukocytosis and elevated cardiac enzymes and inflammatory markers. The cardiac biomarker troponin I was found to have low sensitivity 34% and high specificity 89% and a positive predictive value of 82% for detecting viral myocarditis in one study.
CXR can reveal cardiomegaly in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy.
ECG may reveal ventricular or atrial arrhythmias, acute ST segment changes, and heart blocks. Ischemic cardiomyopathy should be excluded when patient presents with dilated cardiomyopathy.

Cardiac MRI is recommended as the preferred imaging study for patients with clinically suspected acute viral myocarditis by European expert consensus guidelines. PET scan is an option for patients with contraindications to cardiac MRI.

Consider coronary angiography or nuclear stress testing to rule out ischemic cardiomyopathy, especially in patients presenting with ischemic changes in the ECG, positive cardiac enzymes, and decreased left ventricular (LV) function. Gallium 67 scintigraphy may be helpful in identifying patients with acute myocarditis.

Endomyocardial biopsy fulfilling Dallas criteria for myocarditis is the reference standard for diagnosis, but has low sensitivity (10%–15%). Sensitivity of biopsy can be enhanced by immunohistochemical and molecular biological techniques. Sensitivity and specificity of endomyocardial biopsy is 50% and 95.4%, respectively when patients have active myocarditis. Biopsy is recommended for patients who have an acute deterioration in cardiac function and who are not responding to medical therapy, or when other causes of cardiomyopathy are suspected (ie, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia, and other infiltrative cardiomyopathy).
Cardiovascular MR with gadolinium may show delayed enhancement of myocardium. Antimyosin scintigraphy can identify myocardial inflammation.
Cardiomyopathy occurs in approximately 10% to 20% of HIV patients. Consider screening in newly diagnosed HIV patients with echocardiography.
A a novel microRNA found in patients with myocarditis (hsa-miR-Chr8:96) accurately distinguishes patients with myocarditis from those with MI (AUC 0.927).
The clinical spectrum of viral cardiomyopathy varies from asymptomatic to sudden cardiac death, fulminant heart failure, and chronic dilated cardiomyopathy. B
Suspect viral myocarditis in patients with chest pain, palpitations, syncope, dyspnea on exertion, and pedal edema preceded by fever, myalgia.
Initial evaluation includes cardiac enzymes, CXR, ECG, and cardiac echocardiogram.

Treatment is similar to that for systolic heart failure caused by ischemic heart disease: ACEI, ARB, combination of ARB with neprilysin inhibitor, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid antaagonists, and diuretics.
Some patients may require ventricular assist device (VAD), pacemaker, implanted cardioverter defibrillator, or heart transplant.
Patients with significant advanced heart failure findings should be evaluated by a cardiologist who specializes in heart failure care.
Supportive care, pharmacological treatment of arrhythmias, diuretics, and ACEIs for heart failure are the primary therapy for viral cardiomyopathy. A
Immunosuppression should not be used in the routine treatment of viral cardiomyopathy. A

Pharmacological treatment with beta blockers, diuretics, and ACEIs for heart failure are the recommended therapy for viral cardiomyopathy. Aldosterone antagonists are recommended for NYHA Class III-IV patients.

Beta-blockers (especially carvedilol) improve the survival in nonischemic cardiomyopathy inclusive of viral cardiomyopathy. However, a study in children with dilated or congenital cardiomyopathy with decreased LV function did not benefit from carvedilol.

A Cochrane review identified 8 RCTs with 719 patients comparing corticosteroids with an alternative treatment. They found no evidence of mortality benefit, and only a possible benefit in terms of cardiac functional parameters and enzymes.
Digoxin should be used with caution and only in low doses.

Immunosuppression using immune globulin, azathioprine, or cyclosporin has failed to show survival or functional benefit in RCTs and should not be used for routine treatment of viral cardiomyopathy.
IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) therapy response may vary depending upon the type of virus causing cardiomyopathy.

Viral-specific vaccines worked better in measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR); polio; and influenza myocarditis. Further work is underway in this field. Antiviral therapy using interferon-beta is also being studied.
Aspirin and NSAIDs may worsen the acute and subacute phases of myocarditis by decreasing viral clearance, exaggerating cytotoxic response, and coronary artery spasm.
Cardiac transplantation is an option for end stage cardiomyopathy.

Cardiogenic shock can be a consequence of viral myocarditis, and may require emergent mechanical hemodynamic support including intra-aortic balloon pump, percutaneous left ventricular assist device, or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation.
Arteriovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation serves as a bridge to recovery, destination left ventricular assist device implantation, or heart transplantation.
Some patients may require implanted defibrillator, pacemaker, or left ventricular assist device.
Chinese herbal medicines may have an antiarrhythmic effect in viral myocarditis. However, RCTs are lacking.
Patients should have supportive care including oxygen as needed to maintain adequate oxygen saturation.
Avoid exercise and alcohol intake during acute myocarditis.
Admit patients with chest pain, significant ECG changes, elevated cardiac enzymes, worrisome cardiac arrhythmias, or decompensated heart failure.

Patient presenting with fulminant heart failure should be hospitalized and managed with IV inotropic therapy and/or mechanical support. Fulminant myocarditis patients have excellent long-term prognosis.

Patients presenting with syncope, ventricular arrhythmias, and heart blocks should be treated with implantable defibrillator and pacemaker as needed. Defibrillator reduces mortality in selected patients with nonischemic cardiomyopathy inclusive of viral cardiomyopathy.
Patients presenting with fulminant myocarditis should be hemodynamically supported in the ICU and treated with LV assistive devices as required.
Patients with dilated cardiomyopathy can benefit from heart transplant.
Ninety-three percent of patients with fulminant myocarditis are alive without having a heart transplant after 11 years follow-up. B
Forty-five percent of patients with acute myocarditis are alive after 11 years of follow-up. B

Viral myocarditis accounts for about 20% of sudden death in adults younger than 40 years and young athletes.

Prognosis depends on the clinical presentation, type of virus, and pattern of myocardial damage. Coxsackie B myocarditis has benign course. Patients with mixed infections human herpes virus 6/parvo virus B19 and septal involvement have poor prognosis.
Ninety-three percent of patients with fulminant myocarditis are alive without having a heart transplant after 11 years follow-up, compared with only 45% of those with acute myocarditis.

In an historic cohort of patients with HIV-associated viral cardiomyopathy, the 5-year survival rate was observed as 24% compared with 68% in patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy.More recent prognostic data in this group are lacking, but anti-retroviral therapy may improve this relatively poor prognosis.
Children have better prognosis despite presenting with fulminant myocarditis.
Patients initially need follow-up at intervals of 1 to 3 months.
Patients with dilated cardiomyopathy and heart failure need periodic follow-up.
Children with acute myocarditis can be considered for IV immune globulin therapy. In adults, IVIG found to have no benefit. However, in children, no trials are available to assess the benefit.
A small, historically controlled trial of 46 children with acute myocarditis found that survival was 84% with IVIG compared with 60% without (p = .07).
Carvedilol is not effective for children and adolescents with heart failure.
